note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Chapters 3, 4 and 5 are deliberately absent — every lesson in them is still schema v1 with no practises.knowledge, so no payoff could name a real atom, and a stub would destroy the very signal the gap report exists to carry. Chapters 34 and 35 are the second verb tranche and are schema v2 throughout, so their payoffs name real atoms. Chapters 1 and 2 have no schema-v2 terminal consolidation lesson either: their HI-C01/HI-C02 practice lessons are schema v1, so the payoff falls back to the chapter's last lesson by sequence, which in both cases is a Devanagari writing lesson. Those are recorded as kind 'task' and described as hand-writing work rather than dressed up as spoken dialogue.

chapters.title: Greetings
chapters.label: ch:greetings
chapters.canDo: I can greet, thank, and take my leave in Hindi, and write by hand the first Devanagari letters those words are built from.

payoff.summary: Write क and त in stroke order — loop or curl, spine, bar last — then say the stop series back to front along the mouth.

chapters.title: Introducing Yourself
chapters.label: ch:introductions
chapters.canDo: I can give my name and ask for someone else's in Hindi, and write मेरा नाम and नमस्ते by hand.

payoff.summary: Assemble नमस्ते from न, म, स् and ते under a single head-line, then say the bow the word literally names.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Five
chapters.label: ch:hi-numbers-1-5
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to five in Hindi and hear the older Sanskrit shapes still sitting inside तीन, चार and पाँच.

payoff.summary: Say पाँच beside Sanskrit pañca and point to the moon-dot that is all that survives of the lost nasal consonant.

chapters.title: Yes and No
chapters.label: ch:hi-yes-and-no
chapters.canDo: I can say yes and no in Hindi and use नहीं to negate a whole sentence.

payoff.summary: Say नहीं, put it in front of a verb — मैं नहीं जानता — and hear the single PIE *ne behind no, non and nein.

chapters.title: Please
chapters.label: ch:hi-please
chapters.canDo: I can say please in Hindi, both with कृपया and with the polite verb ending everyday speech actually prefers.

payoff.summary: Say कृपया with its vocalic ऋ, unpack it as 'of your compassion', then switch to the everyday बैठिए, 'please sit'.

chapters.title: Sorry
chapters.label: ch:hi-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Hindi with माफ़ कीजिए and reach for its more formal cousin when the moment calls for it.

payoff.summary: Say माफ़ कीजिए as 'please do forgiveness', then क्षमा करें when the setting is formal.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:hi-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name all seven days of the week in Hindi and say which planet each day is named for.

payoff.summary: Recite सोमवार through रविवार end to end, naming Saturn's day and the Sun's day to close the planet-week.

chapters.title: Four Core Colours
chapters.label: ch:hi-core-colours
chapters.canDo: I can name black, white, red and blue in Hindi and say which of them came from Sanskrit and which from Persian.

payoff.summary: Say लाल and नीला beside काला and सफ़ेद, keeping nīla and 'indigo' honestly linked by trade rather than by sound.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.label: ch:hi-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my father, mother, brother and sister in Hindi.

payoff.summary: Say भाई and बहन beside पिता and माता, and name which one is a true cousin of English 'brother' and which is not.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:hi-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Hindi and trace both back to the Sanskrit words they wore down from.

payoff.summary: Say हाथ, then हस्त, then the shape of the change between them: the -st- cluster simplifies and the vowel lengthens.

chapters.title: Seasons
chapters.label: ch:hi-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name all six traditional Indian seasons in Hindi, including the one the four-season frame has no word for.

payoff.summary: Say all six ऋतु in order and point to वर्षा, the monsoon season no Western four-season label maps onto.

chapters.title: Water and Bread
chapters.label: ch:hi-water-and-bread
chapters.canDo: I can ask for water and bread in Hindi and say what पानी literally means.

payoff.summary: Ask for पानी and रोटी, then unpack पानी as 'the drinkable one' — pā, to drink, plus -nīya, fit for.

chapters.title: Months
chapters.label: ch:hi-months
chapters.canDo: I can name the twelve months in Hindi and explain why the festivals move against the Gregorian calendar.

payoff.summary: Say जनवरी through दिसंबर, then name Chaitra and Vaiśākh and explain that the festivals are dated by Vikram Samvat instead.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:hi-noon-and-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say noon and midnight in Hindi and explain the old three-hour pahar hidden inside दोपहर.

payoff.summary: Say दोपहर as 'two pahars' and आधी रात as 'half night', contrasting one built on an old time-unit with one built plainly.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:hi-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can tell someone what o'clock it is in Hindi.

payoff.summary: Say एक बज रहा है and दो बज रहे हैं — the hour striking, exactly as the ghaṇṭā bell once did.

chapters.title: Asking Someone's Age
chapters.label: ch:hi-asking-age
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone's age in Hindi and give my own in the belonging-to-years shape Hindi uses.

payoff.summary: Ask तुम कितने साल के हो? and answer मैं बीस साल का हूँ, with के/का carrying the 'belonging to' work.

chapters.title: Weather
chapters.label: ch:hi-weather
chapters.canDo: I can say what the weather is doing in Hindi and stay out of the बारिश / वर्षा false-friend trap.

payoff.summary: Say मौसम, then गर्मी है and ठंड है, and keep everyday बारिश apart from formal वर्षा despite the resemblance.

chapters.title: Numbers Six to Ten
chapters.label: ch:hi-numbers-six-to-ten
chapters.canDo: I can count from six to ten in Hindi and hear the sound changes that wore the Sanskrit numerals down.

payoff.summary: Trace ṣaṣ → chhah, nava → nau and daśa → das, naming the one change each numeral underwent.

chapters.title: Numbers Eleven to Twenty
chapters.label: ch:hi-numbers-eleven-to-twenty
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Hindi and spot the subtractive nineteen sitting inside the list.

payoff.summary: Count ग्यारह to बीस, then read उन्नीस as 'one less than twenty', the same logic as Latin's ūndēvīgintī.

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:hi-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Hindi and say honestly how far back each word can actually be traced.

payoff.summary: Trace बिल्ली back through biḍālikā to biḍāla, then say out loud where the evidence stops being solid.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:hi-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can name green and yellow in Hindi and trace पीला step by step back to Sanskrit.

payoff.summary: Trace pīta · pītala · pīala · pīlā in order, and flag the drink-to-yellow link as uncertain rather than settled.

chapters.title: Day
chapters.label: ch:hi-day
chapters.canDo: I can say day in Hindi and explain how दिन both is and is not related to Latin's diēs.

payoff.summary: Say दिन, put it and diēs on the same PIE *dyew- root but different branches, then name द्यु/दिव् as the closer cousins.

chapters.title: Night
chapters.label: ch:hi-night
chapters.canDo: I can say night in Hindi and explain why रात and Latin's nox are not cousins at all.

payoff.summary: Trace rātri → ratti → raat, then state the honest twist: unlike दिन and diēs, रात and nox share no root.

chapters.title: Good Night
chapters.label: ch:hi-good-night
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good night in Hindi and say why the phrase uses literary रात्रि rather than everyday रात.

payoff.summary: Say शुभ रात्रि at parting, name the raat / rātri register pair, and trace śubh from 'to shine' to 'auspicious'.

chapters.title: Morning
chapters.label: ch:hi-morning
chapters.canDo: I can say morning in Hindi and recognise सुबह as a Persian-Arabic loan rather than a Sanskrit word.

payoff.summary: Say सुबह, find the ṣ-b-ḥ root it shares with Arabic ṣabāḥ, and name the break from Sanskrit दिन and रात.

chapters.title: Evening
chapters.label: ch:hi-evening
chapters.canDo: I can say evening in Hindi and refuse the tempting but false link between शाम and Sanskrit śyāmā.

payoff.summary: Say शाम, reject the śyāmā resemblance as a false cognate, and pair it with सुबह as two loans from the same source.

chapters.title: Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:hi-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can say afternoon in Hindi using दोपहर in its modern, widened sense.

payoff.summary: Say दोपहर में for 'in the afternoon' — the Chapter 17 word doing a wider job than its etymology promises.

chapters.title: Good Morning
chapters.label: ch:hi-good-morning
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good morning in Hindi and judge when सुप्रभात fits and when नमस्ते is the better choice.

payoff.summary: Say सुप्रभात, split it into su + prabhāt, and set that native Sanskrit dawn against the Persian loan सुबह.

chapters.title: Good Evening
chapters.label: ch:hi-good-evening
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good evening in Hindi and choose between शुभ संध्या and नमस्ते by register.

payoff.summary: Pick शुभ संध्या for a written evening card and नमस्ते for a casual 7 p.m. hello, treating the split as a tendency, not a ban.

chapters.title: Good Afternoon
chapters.label: ch:hi-good-afternoon
chapters.canDo: I can wish someone good afternoon in Hindi and say honestly how rarely शुभ दोपहर is actually used.

payoff.summary: Say शुभ दोपहर with दोपहर in its widened sense, then rank it honestly below नमस्ते/नमस्कार for everyday afternoons.

chapters.title: Four Verbs of the Mind
chapters.label: ch:hi-verbs-of-the-mind
chapters.canDo: I can say what I think, understand, read and write in Hindi, run all four through the present habitual, and say "Sorry, I don't understand" when I need to.

payoff.summary: Run सोचना, समझना, पढ़ना and लिखना through मैं …ता/ती हूँ, spell out मेरा नाम from the letters you first wrote by hand, and name the one meaning — to scratch — that four unrelated families each chose for "write".

chapters.title: Taking, Asking, Helping — and Liking
chapters.label: ch:hi-pasand
chapters.canDo: I can say I take, ask and help in Hindi, build a conjunct verb out of any noun plus करना, and say what I like the way Hindi says it — with the thing liked as the subject and me in the dative.

payoff.summary: Say लेना, पूछना and मदद करना, then turn the sentence inside out: मुझे रोटी पसंद है is bread being pleasing to me, so है agrees with the bread and I move into मुझे — the same inversion Spanish and Italian reached on their own.
